entities.summary:
Robert of Nantes (d. 1254-06-08) was a prominent Cistercian prelate who served as Bishop of Nantes (1236-1240) and later Archbishop of Embrun (1240-1254), playing a crucial role in consolidating papal authority and ecclesiastical rights within the turbulent political landscape of 13th-century France and the broader Latin West. Born around 1200, likely in Saintonge, his career unfolded amidst the struggles between secular rulers and the papacy, particularly during the pontificate of Innocent IV. His life exemplifies the assertive power of the Church in an era marked by intense political maneuvering and the aftermath of major crusades.

His tenure as Bishop of Nantes was characterized by vigorous defense of episcopal prerogatives against the encroachment of secular lords, most notably Peter Mauclerc, Duke of Brittany. Robert challenged the Duke's attempts to control church appointments and properties, leading to significant legal and political confrontations that often required papal intervention. In 1240, Pope Gregory IX elevated him to Archbishop of Embrun, a strategic see in the Dauphiné region. From this position, he continued to serve as a papal legate, participating in critical diplomatic missions, including efforts to secure peace between England and France and to organize support for the Seventh Crusade.
